editorNote: This week’s British computer press brings a new galaxy to the C64 and a proposed rescue for Sinclair.
morningLine: Elite docks on the Commodore 64; Atari courts developers; Dixons holds the Plus/4 below £100.

lead.headline: Elite brings its trading galaxy to the Commodore 64
lead.dek: Firebird’s space-trading adventure gains colour on another home micro, with a few changes at the docking bay.
body: The Commodore 64 has a new galaxy to explore. Martin Croft’s review in the June 20–26 Popular Computing Weekly finds Elite available from Firebird, carrying across the space-trading and combat formula that made it a major BBC and Electron success in 1984. The review establishes its arrival by this week’s issue, rather than a precise launch day.

The familiar ship and control layout remain, but the view is more colourful. Croft counts four colours in the view screens and eight on the displays. His disk copy loads in a reported 30 seconds—a useful observation from the review machine, rather than a promise for every setup.

There is a trade-off in the drawing room. The line graphics run somewhat more slowly than on the BBC version, according to the review, and players can remove the lines marking planetary polar caps to improve speed. The wireframe universe remains the central attraction.

Docking has acquired its own rhythm. The commander accelerates into the approach before the docking computer engages, and can still manoeuvre or fight while the sequence runs. The Blue Danube supplies the accompaniment. The review leaves the price undecided, so the new commander’s official entry ticket is not yet printed here.

stories.headline: Sinclair faces a Maxwell rescue and a smaller role for Sir Clive
body: Sinclair Research is facing a proposed change of control. Reporting an announcement made on Sunday, June 16, Popular Computing Weekly describes a rescue under which a subsidiary of Robert Maxwell’s Pergamon Press–Hollis would take control, Maxwell would become chairman and a new managing director would be appointed.

The plan calls for Hollis to acquire 75 per cent for a nominal sum and raise £12 million through a three-for-one rights issue at £1 a share. Sir Clive would leave the board while remaining life president and research consultant, and would establish a separate technology-research concern.

The report places financing needs at £15 million and stock above £30 million after disappointing post-Christmas sales. Sir Clive’s 80 per cent holding would initially fall to about 20 per cent and eventually about 10 per cent in the account’s continuation. These are the terms of an announced proposal, not a completed takeover.

stories.headline: Atari courts more than 100 British software houses for the ST
body: Atari says more than 100 British software houses will develop for the ST and is selling 520 ST machines to developers. Its ambition is an independent library of roughly 100 titles by September’s Personal Computer World Show—a target for the autumn, not a catalogue already in the shops.

Psion, Precision, Triptych, First Publishing and Hi-Soft confirm work. Psion discusses Chess and possibly Xchange later, while Precision plans Superbase and Superscript for both ST and Amiga. Atari’s Rob Harding describes a roughly even division among business software, utilities and integrated packages, and entertainment.

The timetable still depends on hardware. First Publishing hopes for October titles but explicitly makes that conditional on machine availability. Firebird, Hewson and Beyond have expressed interest without committing; a lively prospectus is not yet a stocked software shelf.

stories.headline: Dixons keeps the Plus/4 below £100 despite Commodore’s bundling push
body: Dixons is keeping the Commodore Plus/4 below £100. The June 20 weekly reports a £99.90 offer with four C16 games, a price already in force for two weeks. That gives the budget buyer a very different proposition from Commodore’s new office bundle.

The £449 Plus/4 Business Pack includes a 1541 disk drive, MPS 801 printer and Impex software as well as the computer. Commodore hopes its bundles will discourage price cutting, but acknowledges that Dixons is free to choose its prices. The retailer has not decided whether to stock the Business Pack.

market.headline: Rescue plans and retail price pressure
market.summary: Sinclair’s proposed Maxwell rescue and Commodore’s bundle strategy put finance beside the shop window. Neither the rescue proposal nor Atari’s autumn software target is a completed transaction or an available catalogue.

worldAnchor.headline: Discovery launches three-satellite mission
worldAnchor.summary: Discovery launched on June 17 with seven crew, including Sultan Salman Al-Saud and Patrick Baudry. STS-51G carries the MORELOS-A, ARABSAT-A and TELSTAR-3D communications satellites for deployment.

bbsNote.headline: Commodore pushes cheaper modems and wider online services

posts.text: Goheen describes a Hayes-like 1200-baud smartmodem and says Commodore will ultimately break $100, while declining to specify initial pricing.

posts.platform: CompuServe, Dow Jones, The Source, Delphi, Playnet and TeleLearning
posts.text: Goheen names relationships and starter packs involving Compuserve, Dow Jones, The Source, Delphi, Playnet and TeleLearning, and discusses educational databases. A separate Commodore service remains an exploratory possibility.
GE’s 3-8200 offers acoustic/direct-connect 300-baud operation, optional 9-volt battery power and a $119.95 list price in June’s Gazette.

bbsNote.summary: In June’s Gazette interview, Commodore software director Paul Goheen places telecomputing at the heart of the company’s plans. A sub-$100 1670 is an eventual ambition, not an established shelf price.

curiosity.headline: A poet’s electronic novel arrives as a hardback with a disk
curiosity.summary: Mindwheel blurs the line between bookshelf and disk library.
curiosity.detail: June’s Gazette explains that Synapse’s electronic novels put a disk in the back of a hardback book; players must learn information from the printed book. Robert Pinsky developed Mindwheel from the wheel concept in his own poetry.

undergroundDesk.headline: Prestel hacking test case adjourned
undergroundDesk.dek: June reporting follows the opening Bow Street hearing; charges remain allegations.
body: Popular Computing Weekly reports that proceedings against Stephen Gold and Robert Schifreen opened at Bow Street on June 12 and were adjourned to July 4. The opening hearing predates this issue week; the account appears in the June 20 weekly.

The paper reports five additional charges against Gold and four against Schifreen, and links the case to the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981. It presents a test of hacking’s legal status, not a verdict. No crew or board is identified in this report.
